subject: ela
cluster: Range of reading and level of text complexity
intro: Each problem gives you a full literary passage, scene, or poem. Read the whole thing carefully, then answer the question in a complete sentence. These passages are longer and more layered than usual, so you will need to hold the entire excerpt in mind and combine several details before you decide on your answer. Watch out for figurative language, and remember that the best answer is supported by the passage as a whole, not by a single sentence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

For most of the season, Eli rode the bench and clapped harder than anyone. He memorized the names of every player who got to start, and he learned the coach's signals so well that he could call the next play under his breath before it happened. At practice he stayed late, fielding ground balls until the field lights buzzed off. When the team's best shortstop sprained an ankle in the final inning of the championship game, the coach scanned the bench and pointed at Eli. Eli's hands went cold. He trotted to the position he had studied all year but never played in a real game. The first ball came hard and low, skipping over the dirt. He did not think. His glove was already there. He threw to first a half second before the runner arrived, and the crowd's roar washed over him like a wave he had been swimming toward all season.

Which statement best summarizes the central idea of the passage?
items.answer: Eli's quiet, year-long preparation pays off when he finally gets his chance and succeeds, showing that patient effort readies a person for the moment they have been waiting for.

steps: Track the whole arc: Eli watches, studies signals, and practices late all season, then is suddenly put in and makes the play.
The central idea must cover both halves: the long preparation AND the payoff, not just one moment.
His success on the first ball ('His glove was already there') is a direct result of all the studying and late practice, so the gist is that patient preparation readied him for his chance.
Reject summaries that focus only on the sprained ankle or only on the final throw, since those are single details, not the main point.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The lighthouse keeper, old Mr. Okafor, had not spoken to the villagers in years. They called him the hermit of the point and warned children away from his gate. But every storm, without fail, his lamp turned through the dark, slow and steady, sweeping the cliffs so the fishing boats could find the harbor mouth. One winter night the storm was the worst anyone could remember. The power lines snapped and the village went black, house by house, until the only light for miles was the patient circle of the lighthouse, turning and turning. In the morning the fishermen counted their boats. Every one had come home. No one ever thanked Mr. Okafor, and he never asked them to. He simply climbed the stairs the next evening, as he always did, and lit the lamp again.

What theme does the passage most fully develop?
items.answer: Quiet, faithful service can protect and benefit others even when it goes unrecognized and unthanked.

steps: Notice the contrast: the village rejects Mr. Okafor as a hermit, yet he keeps every boat safe through the storm.
Key details build the theme: his lamp turns 'without fail,' he is never thanked, and he 'never asked them to,' yet he lights the lamp again.
Combine these to see the message is about steady, unrewarded service that still does good for others.
Reject readings that say the village learned to love him (never stated) or that he is bitter (the text shows quiet duty, not resentment).

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Maya had been the loudest voice in the room since the fifth grade. She organized the food drive, ran for class office, and never once let a silence sit longer than a breath. So when the new student, Tomas, arrived speaking little English and eating lunch alone, everyone assumed Maya would sweep him into her crowd within a day. Instead, she did something none of them expected. She sat down beside him and said nothing at all. She unwrapped her sandwich, slid half of it across the table, and pointed at the cafeteria mural, raising her eyebrows as if asking a question. Tomas almost smiled. The next day she brought a small notebook and they traded drawings instead of words. By the end of the week, the loudest girl in school had become, for one quiet friendship, completely silent, and she had never seemed kinder.

What can the reader most reasonably infer about how Maya has changed in this passage?
items.answer: Maya learns that kindness sometimes means setting aside her usual loud, take-charge way and meeting someone quietly on his own terms.

steps: Establish her starting trait: she is the loudest voice, organizes everything, and never lets silence sit.
Notice the surprising shift: with Tomas she says nothing, shares food, and trades drawings instead of words.
The inference combines the contrast: her growth is realizing that quiet, patient kindness can matter more than her usual loud approach.
Reject 'she became shy' (overstated, she is still herself elsewhere) and 'she gave up leadership' (not supported; this is one friendship, not a personality erasure).

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then answer the question.

The River's Lesson

The river never argues with the stone,
it simply leans against it, year on year,
and though the stone seems mighty, hard, and grown,
the water wears a softer pathway clear.
No hammer falls, no thunder splits the rock,
no single day reveals the work begun,
yet grain by grain, around the steady clock,
the river writes the canyon, one by one.
So do not scorn the small and patient deed,
the gentle pull that never seems to win,
for what looks weak against a stubborn need
may be the very force that wears it thin.

What does the poem suggest through the image of the river and the stone?
items.answer: Gentle, persistent effort over a long time can overcome even something that seems far stronger, so small steady actions should not be underestimated.

steps: Read the central image figuratively: the river is soft and the stone seems 'mighty,' yet the water slowly carves the canyon.
Phrases like 'grain by grain' and 'year on year' stress that the change comes from patience, not force.
The final lines turn the image into advice: 'do not scorn the small and patient deed,' so the poem's message is that quiet persistence can wear down what looks unbeatable.
Reject the literal misread that the poem is just describing how canyons form geologically, and reject 'force always wins,' since the poem praises gentleness over hammering.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Grandfather kept the garden the way other people kept secrets. Every spring he turned the same dark soil, pressed the same seeds into rows only he understood, and refused all offers of help. When I asked why he never let the neighbors plant beside him, he only said, "A garden remembers the hands that tend it." That summer he grew ill and could not kneel in the dirt. The rows went ragged. Weeds rose where tomatoes should have. I expected him to grieve the loss, but instead he handed me his worn gloves and walked me out to the beds. He showed me which leaves to pinch and which to leave, his voice slow but certain. By August the garden was green again, tended now by my hands. I understood at last what he had been planting all those years, and it was not only vegetables.

What does the grandfather's statement, 'A garden remembers the hands that tend it,' most likely mean in this passage?
items.answer: A garden carries the care and effort of the person who tends it, and through that care the grandfather is passing on his knowledge and connection to the next generation.

steps: Treat the saying as figurative, not literal: a garden cannot really remember, so it stands for something deeper.
Connect it to the ending, where the grandfather teaches the narrator and says he was 'planting' more than vegetables.
Combining the saying with the lesson shows it means the gardener's care lives on in the garden and is handed down to whoever tends it next.
Reject the literal reading that plants have memory, and reject 'he did not trust the neighbors' gardening,' which is not the point of the saying.

Read the passage, then answer the question.

The debate team had practiced for a month, and Priya had practiced longest of all. She knew the rebuttals cold. But on the morning of the tournament, her teammate Daniel froze at the podium, his notecards trembling, the words simply gone. The judges began to write. Priya could have let him fail; the rankings counted each speaker separately, and his stumble would not lower her own score. Instead she leaned forward and whispered the first line of his argument, just loud enough for him to catch. His shoulders dropped. He found the thread again and spoke the rest himself, steadier with each sentence. Their team did not place first that day. But on the bus home, Daniel sat beside Priya and did not say thank you, because some things are understood without being said, and she only handed him half her sandwich and looked out the window, smiling.

What can the reader most reasonably infer about Priya from her actions in this passage?
items.answer: Priya values her teammate's success and their friendship more than her own individual ranking, so she chooses to help Daniel even though it does not benefit her score.

steps: Note the key tension the text supplies: helping Daniel would not raise Priya's own separate score, so she gains nothing personally.
She helps anyway by whispering his line and later sharing her sandwich and smiling.
Combine these details to infer her character: she puts loyalty and her teammate above her own ranking.
Reject 'Priya wanted to win first place' (the text shows she sacrifices ranking) and 'Priya felt sorry for herself,' which the smiling ending contradicts.

items.prompt:
Read the scene, then answer the question.

[A cramped attic. Rain taps the window. NORA stands holding a dusty box. Her brother, SAM, sits on a trunk.]

SAM: You can't keep all of it. The movers come Tuesday.

NORA: I'm not keeping all of it. Just this. (She lifts an old kite, its paper torn, the string a tangle.)

SAM: That thing never even flew right.

NORA: It flew once. The day Dad ran the whole length of the beach so it would catch. Remember? He was out of breath for an hour.

SAM: (quieter) I'd forgotten the beach.

NORA: That's why I'm keeping it. (She wraps the kite carefully in a cloth.) Not because it flies. Because he ran.

SAM: (standing, after a pause) ... Put it in my box. It'll be safer there.

What does Sam's final line, 'Put it in my box. It'll be safer there,' most reveal about the change in him during the scene?
items.answer: Sam comes to share Nora's feeling that the kite is worth keeping for its memory of their father, shifting from wanting to discard it to wanting to protect it.

steps: Track Sam at the start: he dismisses the kite, saying it 'never even flew right' and that they cannot keep everything.
Notice the turn when Nora reminds him of the beach and their father, and Sam grows 'quieter' and admits he had forgotten.
His final offer to keep the kite safe shows he now values it too, so he has shifted from rejecting the kite to protecting the memory.
Reject 'Sam still thinks the kite is useless' (his action contradicts it) and 'Sam is only being practical about space,' since the emotional pause shows feeling, not logistics.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

When the carnival came to the dusty town of Harlow, it brought a Ferris wheel that lit the night like a fallen constellation. Children pressed their faces to fences. But Cara, who was twelve and tired of being told she was too small for things, walked straight to the tallest ride and got in line. The attendant looked her over and waved her through. As the car climbed, the town shrank beneath her until the streets she had walked a thousand times looked like the lines on her own palm. She could see the whole shape of Harlow at once, the river curling past it, the road stretching off toward places she had never been. For one slow turn at the top, the wind cool on her face, Cara understood that the town was small and the world was not, and that she would not always be small either.

Which statement best expresses the theme that emerges by the end of the passage?
items.answer: Gaining a wider view can change how a person sees their small world and help them imagine the larger life and possibilities ahead of them.

steps: Notice Cara's frustration at being called 'too small for things,' which sets up the meaning of the ride.
At the top she sees the whole town shrink and the road stretching to 'places she had never been.'

The closing realization ties the literal high view to a figurative one: the town is small, the world is not, and she will not always be small, so the theme is about new perspective opening up possibility.
Reject 'carnivals are exciting for children' (too narrow, surface detail) and 'Cara is afraid of heights,' which the calm wonder of the scene contradicts.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The old fisherman, Bao, had hauled nets from the bay for fifty years, and the bay had given him a hard, sun-creased face and hands like rope. The younger fishermen laughed at how he still mended his nets by hand when machines could do it faster. They laughed less the morning the storm trapped two boys on the sandbar as the tide rose. The newer boats had engines that stalled in the churning shallows. But Bao knew the bay the way he knew his own breathing, the hidden channel where the water ran calm even in a gale. He rowed in by hand, the old way, and brought the boys back wet and shaking but alive. He said nothing about it afterward. He only sat on the dock that evening, mending a net, as the same young men who had laughed now watched him with new and silent respect.

What does the phrase 'hands like rope' suggest about Bao, and how does the passage as a whole develop its meaning?
items.answer: The phrase suggests Bao's hands are tough and weathered from a lifetime of hard work, and the passage develops this into the idea that his old-fashioned experience makes him stronger and wiser than the younger men realize.

steps: Read 'hands like rope' figuratively: it means hands made tough and weathered by years of labor, not literally made of rope.
Connect this to the larger contrast between Bao's old ways and the young men's machines.
When the engines stall, Bao's hard-earned knowledge saves the boys, so the figurative image of toughness pays off in the plot and earns him respect.
Reject the literal misread that his hands are actually rope-like in shape only, and reject 'the young men were right to laugh,' which the rescue reverses.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

For years Lucia had told herself she would learn to swim 'someday.' She was the one who held the towels, who watched from the shallow end, who clapped when her friends dove. On her thirteenth birthday her cousin offered to teach her in the calm cove behind the house, and Lucia almost said no the way she always did. But this time she heard herself say yes. The first lesson was clumsy. She swallowed water, her arms thrashed, and she clung to the dock more than once. The second lesson was a little less clumsy. By the end of the summer she could cross the cove and back, slow but sure, her cousin floating beside her. She was not fast and she was not graceful. But she was no longer the girl who only held the towels, and the word 'someday' had finally turned into a day with a date.

Which statement best summarizes how Lucia changes over the course of the passage?
items.answer: Lucia moves from endlessly putting off learning to swim to actually committing and gradually succeeding, turning a vague 'someday' into a real accomplishment through persistence.

steps: Establish her starting state: she only watches, holds towels, and tells herself 'someday.'
Mark the turning point when she says yes, and follow the gradual progress across lessons.
The ending shows her crossing the cove and the word 'someday' becoming 'a day with a date,' so the summary must capture the shift from delay to follow-through.
Reject 'Lucia became a fast, graceful swimmer' (the text says she was neither) and 'Lucia spent the summer watching her friends,' which describes only her old self.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

The class hamster, Biscuit, escaped on a Friday, and by Monday everyone had given up except Theo. The teacher said the cage door must have been left ajar over the weekend. The other students searched the obvious places once, found nothing, and moved on. Theo did not. He noticed the trail of sunflower-seed shells leading behind the bookshelf, the faint scratching from inside the wall vent, the way the classroom rabbit kept staring at the same low cabinet. He did not announce any of this. He simply set a small dish of seeds by the cabinet each morning and waited. On Wednesday, when the others had forgotten Biscuit entirely, Theo opened the cabinet door and there, curled in a nest of shredded paper, blinked the missing hamster, plump and unbothered. He carried it back to the cage without a word, as if finding lost things were simply what patient eyes were for.

What can the reader most reasonably infer about why Theo succeeds where the other students fail?
items.answer: Theo succeeds because he observes carefully and keeps trying patiently while the others give up quickly, so his attentiveness and persistence let him find the hamster.

steps: Contrast the behaviors: the others search once and move on, but Theo keeps watching.
Gather Theo's specific actions: he notices the seed shells, the scratching, the rabbit's stare, and patiently sets out seeds each day.
Combine these to infer the cause of his success: careful observation plus persistence, which the closing line about 'patient eyes' confirms.
Reject 'Theo was lucky' (the text shows deliberate clues he followed) and 'the teacher told Theo where to look,' which never happens.

items.prompt:
Read the poem, then answer the question.

The Last Apple

One apple clung to the orchard tree
when all the rest had fallen down,
high on a branch where the wind blew free,
the last red coin on a bare brown crown.
The pickers came and called it lost,
too high to reach, not worth the climb,
and left it there to face the frost,
forgotten by the end of time.
But a small bird found it, bright and whole,
when winter pinched the world to bone,
and what the pickers had let go
became the one warm meal she'd known.

What is the most reasonable interpretation of the poem's central idea?
items.answer: Something other people dismiss as worthless or not worth the effort can turn out to be exactly what someone else needs, so value depends on more than first appearances.

steps: Follow the apple's story: the pickers judge it 'not worth the climb' and leave it, calling it lost.
Notice the reversal in the final stanza: the bird finds the same apple and it becomes her 'one warm meal.'
Combine the two views to read the central idea figuratively: what some discard as worthless can be precious to another, so worth is not fixed by one judgment.
Reject the literal misread that the poem is only about an apple going to waste, and reject 'pickers should work harder,' which misses the bird's role entirely.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Aunt Rosa's kitchen was always loud, always crowded, always smelling of garlic and rain on warm bread. As a small child I thought the noise was the point, the bumping elbows and the three conversations stacked on top of one another. It was only after she was gone, after the kitchen fell quiet and someone else owned the house, that I understood. The noise had never been the point. The point had been that no one in that kitchen was ever alone. Rosa had a gift for gathering, for setting an extra plate without asking, for making the lonely feel expected. People came in cold and left warm, and not only from the soup. I did not know what she had given us until the giving stopped, and the silence where her kitchen used to be taught me, too late, exactly what to listen for.

Which statement best captures the central insight the narrator reaches by the end of the passage?
items.answer: The narrator realizes that the true value of Aunt Rosa's kitchen was the belonging and welcome she gave people, a gift the narrator fully understood only after it was gone.

steps: Notice the narrator's early misunderstanding: as a child he thought the noise itself was the point.
Track the correction: 'The noise had never been the point,' the point was that no one was ever alone and the lonely felt expected.
Combine with the ending about understanding 'too late' to capture the insight: Rosa's real gift was belonging, recognized only after she was gone.

Reject 'the kitchen was loud and crowded' (a surface detail, the narrator's rejected first idea) and 'the soup was what kept people warm,' which the text directly corrects with 'not only from the soup.'

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Marcus had built the model bridge for the science fair entirely from toothpicks and glue, and he had built it to win. He had read about trusses and tension, tested three designs, and chosen the strongest. On the morning of the fair, the boy at the next table, Owen, was nearly in tears: his own bridge had collapsed in his backpack and he had nothing to show. Marcus knew the judges scored each project against the others. Helping Owen could only hurt his own chances. He looked at his careful bridge, then at Owen's pile of broken pieces, then at the clock. There was an hour left. Marcus pulled his chair around to Owen's table, spread out the broken toothpicks, and said, "Okay. Tension here, weight there. We can fix this." They did not both win. But when the bridges were tested and Owen's held its load, Owen turned to Marcus with a look that no ribbon could have bought, and Marcus found he did not mind at all.

What can the reader most reasonably infer about what Marcus values, based on the passage as a whole?
items.answer: Marcus values helping a friend in need and the relationship more than winning, choosing to share his knowledge even though it could hurt his own chances at the fair.

steps: Set up the conflict the text provides: helping Owen 'could only hurt his own chances' because projects are scored against each other.
Marcus still chooses to help, rebuilding Owen's bridge with his hard-won knowledge.
The ending, where Marcus 'did not mind at all' that he did not win, confirms he values the friendship and helping over the prize.
Reject 'Marcus only cared about winning the fair' (his choice disproves it) and 'Marcus was not confident in his own bridge,' which contradicts that he built it to win and tested three designs.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer the question.

Every autumn the geese crossed over our valley, and every autumn my grandmother stopped whatever she was doing to watch them go. She would stand at the window with her hands still wet from the dishes, following the long, wavering V until it thinned into nothing over the southern hills. "They always know," she would say, "when it's time to leave, and they're never sorry to go." I was young and thought it a strange thing to envy, a flock of birds. It was only the autumn she packed her own small suitcase, the autumn she moved at last to the warm coast she had talked about for thirty years, that I understood. She had spent a long life staying for other people, and the geese had been her promise to herself that someday she, too, would follow the season she belonged to. On the morning she left, she did not look back at the house. She looked up.

What does the image of the geese most likely represent in this passage, and how does the ending develop that meaning?
items.answer: The geese represent the grandmother's longing to finally leave and live for herself, and the ending shows her keeping that promise by moving to the coast and looking up at the geese instead of back at the house.

steps: Read the geese figuratively through the grandmother's words: they 'always know when it's time to leave' and are 'never sorry to go.'
Connect this to the revelation that she had 'spent a long life staying for other people' and the geese were 'her promise to herself.'
The ending develops the meaning: she packs her own suitcase and on leaving 'did not look back at the house, she looked up,' mirroring the geese and fulfilling the longing.
Reject the literal reading that the passage is simply about migrating birds, and reject 'the grandmother dislikes her family,' since staying for others is shown as love, not resentment.
